title: Fed Chair Warsh Rejects Political Pressure After Keeping Rates Steady Ahead of Midterms
snippet: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh forcefully rejected claims that political calculations influenced the central bank's decision to pause interest rates just days before the midterm elections.
content:
WASHINGTON — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh forcefully rejected claims that political calculations influenced the central bank’s decision to leave interest rates unchanged this week, brushing aside growing pressure from the White House and Capitol Hill ahead of upcoming midterm elections.

Addressing reporters at a press conference following the Federal Open Market Committee's policy decision, Warsh repeatedly deflected attempts to pull him into Washington's partisan skirmishes. "Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh stated firmly. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics."

Deflecting Oval Office Criticism

The central bank chief’s nonpolitical stance was tested throughout the briefing. Journalists repeatedly asked Warsh about persistent attacks from President Donald Trump, who has argued that interest rates are too high and labeled Fed policymakers as "political." Warsh declined to engage, stating he would not respond to quotes from public officials.

Warsh also distanced the central bank from White House actions, including planned congressional proceedings targeting Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook. Asked if he or the Fed institutionally would participate in the hearing, Warsh remarked, "Not to my knowledge."

Bipartisan Reaction in Washington

Despite Warsh's efforts to maintain institutional neutrality, politicians on both sides of the aisle quickly weighed in on the decision to hold rates steady. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, a Republican, called for borrowing costs to come down soon to support American families.

Meanwhile, Senate Democrats pointed the finger back at the White House. Senator Elizabeth Warren argued in a statement that while working families deserve lower rates and reduced costs, the administration's actions remain the primary obstacle.

Markets Anticipate Future Rate Actions

Despite public calls from lawmakers for immediate rate relief, financial markets are bracing for potential monetary tightening. According to data from the CME FedWatch Tool, traders priced in a greater than 80% chance on Wednesday that the central bank will raise interest rates by a quarter-point at its December meeting as policymakers remain focused on driving inflation down to their 2% target.
